The Social Contract is perhaps the most famous idea of Locke's philosophy. According to Locke, the state derives its just powers from the consent of the governed, and that these powers are legitimate only as long as they continue to serve the common good. In other words, citizens trust the state to protect their property, life, and liberties, in exchange for the state providing certain other things, particularly the protection of life, liberty, and security. This is the basis of his theory of government, according to which the people themselves constitute the sovereign power, and it thus belongs to them to form and govern their state.

The self-determination of individual citizens is important for Locke, and he has proposed several ways in which this notion can be translated into practice. One idea is to give all citizens the right to equal representation in their constitutional assemblies, which would enable them to propose reforms to the state that benefit their own interests. In a second place, Locke has proposed to establish a direct democracy in which people are chosen according to their individual interests and abilities and thus able to participate on a local level in the management of state affairs.

Locke stresses a connection between the individual and the state, and has thus argued that for a system of government to be just the citizens ought to depend on the legitimacy, to such an extent, that it would be irrational for anyone to reject it. This view is connected to other liberal positions in that Locke was an enthusiasticponent of private property rights, but restricted in his concept of individual freedom by his emphasis on the need for the state to protect the collective good. To Locke it was not acceptable that any individual might deliberately jeopardize his fellow citizens' safety by a particular action, but that it was sufficient that each one be satisfied with having his freedom protected, as this entails a necessary kind of cooperation amongst everyone.

Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) is a type of injury that occurs to the brain caused by an external force, such as a blow, jolt, or violent shaking of the head to body. When the head collides with an object, that object usually serves as a shock absorber, protecting the brain, but in some cases, that object can become lodged within the skull and disrupt the normal function of one or more brain cells.

The effects of a TBI depend on many factors - the type of brain cell that is impaired, the speed and extent of the impact, as well as whether or not there are other injuries – and may last for many months, years or even a lifetime. There is an ever-growing body of literature studying the different symptoms that result from a TBI to help determine whether someone suffered brain damage. These include:

Memory issues – Memory problems stemming from a TBI can come in many varieties, but most commonly include difficulties remembering events that happened years ago, as well as problems in retaining details about personal experiences or recent conversations. 

Foggy thinking – Although less common, patients with TBI might report a decline in their perception of time and events later in the day. This condition is termed Aspatial Disorder.

Depression – Like memory problems, symptoms of depression will also vary. Some patients will get depressed or forget things as though they had Alzheimer’s disease, some patients will only experience these symptoms when they feel particularly anxious, confused or “not in their head”.

Difficulty moving – Due to weakened language centers in the brain, some people with a TBI have trouble picking up small objects or walking or talking on the phone. However, the extent to which this impairment is present varies greatly.

Speech problems – Speech problems are relatively common. This can manifest as difficulty in understanding speech or comprehension, mispronunciation, loss of fluency, voice inflections, or altered intonation, pacing or rhythm of speech, or loss of fullness and authority in speech.

Speech sounds or words may appear scrambled; some patients cannot pronounce consonants correctly, whilst others may have trouble with vowels.

Visual problems – A major problem in patients with a TBI may be trouble recognizing faces and making out shapes and lines in space.

Affect disturbances – Affect disorders, such as anxiety, fear, agitation and irritability may also be possible complications, resulting from the brain being more sensitive to certain stimuli.

It is very important to have any such injury assessed quickly by a health care provider for accurate diagnosis and rehabilitation.

2. Motor cells: These take information from what we see and hear, translate it into muscle movement or action, and in general help us to move our body or interact with the environment.

3. Cerebellar cells: These are concerned with balance and coordination of motion, which can be disrupted following a TBI and can affect walking, posture and balance. 

Each cell type plays a vital role in the functioning of our brains, and any disruption in one of them can have lasting effects on our motor functions, attention span and cognitive skills. However, the extent to which each cell type is affected by a TBI can vary greatly greatly depending on the severity and location of an injury. 

There is also some evidence that the presence of cerebellar damage following a TBI may contribute to other cognitive issues later in life such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), impaired memory and other cognitive problems.

For more severe brain injuries, there may be persistent impact to cognitive function and motor function. However, with the right treatment and rehabilitation, these patients are able to live healthy, normal lives with various limitations and symptoms depending on how severe the injury is.

Unfortunately, there are many factors that impact the potential for complete recovery from a TBI. There could be a combination of structural, chemical and neurologic (brain function) factors that may influence a long-term prognosis, as well as other factors like age, pre-existing brain disease history, degree of cognitive impairments, and type of injury.

It's also worth noting that while most individuals recover from a traumatic brain injury, the prognosis can differ greatly depending on how severe the injury is, and specific cases can be very complicated, requiring specialized care from a team of health care providers, including neurologists, orthopedists, physical therapists, neuropsychologists and psychiatrists.
